title: Repairing the world
hook: Luria's cosmic tikkun later became a word for social justice

segments.voice: Yesterday, gathering sparks: each good act frees one from its husk and lifts it home. Your line was repair a shard. What small thing did you mend? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-six.

Near the end of the service in the Jewish prayer book stands a prayer called Aleinu. Toward its close is a hope, and in Hebrew it reads l'taken olam b'malchut Shaddai: to set the world right under the kingdom of the Almighty. Today, that short phrase, tikkun olam, turns up on synagogue banners, on school volunteer days, on the side of a food drive. How did a line from a prayer, and a teaching about broken vessels, end up on a sign by the canned goods? It has quite a road behind it. Today's words.

segments.voice: Repairing the world. Tikkun olam. Follow the phrase four steps down its road. First, the law. In the Mishnah, the rabbis make certain rulings, they say, for the sake of tikkun ha'olam. Rules about how a divorce document is written, so no one is trapped by a careless name. A rule that captives are not ransomed for more than they're worth; one reason later readers give is that kidnapping shouldn't become a business. Here, repairing the world means keeping society fair and in working order. Second, the prayer. In the Aleinu, the phrase lifts its eyes. It becomes a hope for the whole world, set right under God's kingship. Not a rule anymore, a horizon. Third, Luria. In his teaching, tikkun becomes cosmic. The vessels broke; the sparks fell. Every commandment and every kind act gathers a spark and mends a piece of what shattered. Repair isn't only for society now. It's for creation itself, and every person has a share in it. Fourth, today. In more recent times, tikkun olam has become a common name for work for justice: feeding the hungry, caring for the earth, standing up for people pushed aside. Some teachers welcome that wide use. Others ask that it keep its roots in the commandments and in prayer. Both are Jewish voices, and both are part of the phrase's story now. Read this way, what ties the four together is the sense that the world is not finished, and that people's hands belong in the finishing. A rule, a prayer, a spark, a sandwich handed across a table.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: link one small act to the bigger picture. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one small thing you did recently or will do today: holding a door, paying someone on time, returning a cart, calling a parent. Hold it for a moment, just as it is. Now widen the view. Who did it touch? Who does that person go on to touch? Let the picture spread, like rings on water, until your small act looks like one stitch in something much larger. Then come back to the one act, and rest there. The bell holds the time.
Repairing the world. Tikkun olam: a phrase that runs from the Mishnah's fair rulings, through the Aleinu and Luria's mending of creation, to work for justice today. Today's words.
Your line: repair the world. Today, do one ordinary good thing, and name to yourself, quietly, the bigger repair it belongs to. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Tikkun olam is spoken of in Jewish schools, synagogues and community groups as a reason for charity and justice work, while the phrase also stays in the Aleinu prayer said in services.
